pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Evidence-Based Classification (justifying with characteristics)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y6 'Living things and their habitats'):** pupils give reasons for classifying plants and animals based on specific characteristics.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 'Engaging in argument from evidence'):** the US standards don't teach taxonomy here, but the skill — justifying a claim (classification) with observational evidence — is exactly the NGSS argument-from-evidence practice; DfE Y6 is the content anchor.

- **Operational details:** The PROCEDURAL, argumentative capstone of the classification spine: not just placing an organism in a group, but GIVING REASONS — citing specific observable characteristics as evidence to justify the decision, and explaining which characteristics distinguish two similar organisms. Pupils must (a) classify an unfamiliar organism and state the evidence, (b) compare two look-alikes and name the distinguishing characteristic, and (c) justify with at least two pieces of observational evidence. The core move is separating decisive/diagnostic characteristics (has a backbone; makes its own food) from irrelevant ones (colour, size), and constructing a defensible argument rather than an assertion. This is where classification becomes scientific reasoning: a claim backed by evidence.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (relational to formal argument). Pupils build an evidence-backed justification and weigh which characteristics are diagnostic. Success = classifies an unfamiliar organism citing two decisive characteristics and explains why they, not surface features, settle it.
bestPractices: Demand at least two pieces of decisive evidence per classification — a reason, not just a placement — to hit the 'give reasons' standard.
Teach the difference between diagnostic characteristics (has a backbone, makes own food) and irrelevant ones (colour, size, where it lives) using look-alike pairs.
Use convergent look-alikes (dolphin/shark, bat/bird, whale/fish) so pupils must reject shared features and find the distinguishing one.
Model the claim–evidence–reasoning structure explicitly: 'It's a mammal (claim) because it feeds young on milk and breathes air (evidence), and only mammals do both (reasoning).'
Have pupils critique a wrong justification (one built on a shared/irrelevant feature) to sharpen what counts as good evidence.
keyRepresentations: Evidence cards (observable features) pinned to justify a classification claim
Two-look-alike comparison with shared features greyed and the distinguishing feature highlighted
Claim–evidence–reasoning frame for a classification statement
Diagnostic-vs-irrelevant feature sort (decisive characteristics vs distractors)
commonMisconceptions: Justifying with shared features that don't distinguish (a dolphin is a fish 'because it has fins and lives in the sea') — citing non-diagnostic evidence.
Treating classification as a guess or assertion rather than a claim that needs evidence.
Using irrelevant characteristics (colour, size, name) as if they were classifying features.
Giving only one reason, or restating the group name, instead of citing specific distinguishing characteristics.

learn.summary: For learners aged 10–11, build the skill of justifying a biological classification with evidence: not just placing an organism in a group, but giving at least two specific, observable, diagnostic characteristics as reasons, and distinguishing those from features that two similar organisms share. The core move is separating characteristics that are decisive for the comparison being made (e.g. has a backbone, for vertebrate vs invertebrate; makes its own food, for green plants vs animals; breathes air with lungs rather than gills, for dolphin vs shark, though not unique to mammals; feeds young on milk, for mammals) from irrelevant or merely shared ones (colour, size, where it lives, 'swims'). This turns classification into a claim backed by evidence — an instance of argument from evidence. Activities span constructing and defending a justification, a worked-example comparison of look-alikes, and selected-response checks of what counts as decisive evidence.

activities.title: Classification detective: prove the placement
feedback: If evidence cited is shared by both look-alikes (fins, lives in the sea), point out both animals have it: 'The shark has every one of these too — so do they decide the case?' Steer to a feature present in one group and absent in the other.
If only one reason is given, prompt: 'What is a second, independent piece of evidence you can actually SEE?'
If habitat or surface resemblance is used ('lives in water, so it's a fish'), ask 'Do other groups also live in water? So does that really prove it's a fish?'

Try the covering test: ask 'If you covered up everything except this one feature, could you still tell which group it belongs to?' If yes, it is a diagnostic feature; covering a shared feature like fins changes nothing.
When two decisive, distinguishing features are pinned, confirm the argument is complete: the claim now rests on evidence that the claimed group has and the look-alike's group lacks.
activities.rationale: The DfE Y6 standard requires pupils to give reasons for classifying based on specific characteristics; an evidence-marshalling task where the learner must cite and defend decisive features directly rehearses that 'give reasons' objective and the argument-from-evidence practice. A convergent look-alike pair (dolphin/shark) forces rejection of shared features, surfacing the diagnostic-vs-shared distinction.
sourceClaims: DfE Y6 'Living things and their habitats' requires pupils to give reasons for classifying plants and animals based on specific characteristics.
learnerActions: Examine an unfamiliar organism (photo or description — e.g. a pangolin or an axolotl) and collect the features it actually shows. A pangolin is covered in scales, but it has some hair on its face and underside, and the description says it feeds its young on milk, so it is a mammal. An axolotl has a backbone and external gills, but fish share both. Its four legs with toes and its moist, scaleless skin are the features that point to amphibian.
Decide which group it belongs to and file it there.
Pin at least TWO features that justify the decision — reasons, not just a placement.
Then meet a decoy pair: a dolphin beside a shark. First try to justify using 'lives in the sea, streamlined, has fins'; notice these features are shared by BOTH animals so they decide nothing.

Search for the features that actually separate them — the dolphin breathes air with lungs through a blowhole while the shark uses gills, and the dolphin feeds its young on milk while the shark does not — and use those to settle that the dolphin is a mammal and the shark is a fish.
State the full argument: claim (it's a mammal), evidence (feeds young on milk, breathes air), reasoning (only mammals do both).
activities.intendedInsight: A scientific classification is an argument built on distinguishing evidence, not a guess from surface looks; features two look-alikes share cannot decide between them.

activities.title: Defend it: taxonomist challenge dialogue
feedback: When the learner cites a decisive, non-shared feature, the challenger concedes: 'Your group has that feature and the look-alike's group does not — that settles it.'
When a shared or irrelevant feature is offered, the challenger presses: 'But the other animal has that too — try again.'
If the learner restates the group name as its own reason, ask them to name something they can actually observe.
activities.rationale: Because the target is giving and defending reasons, a Socratic challenge can press the learner to justify and to abandon non-diagnostic evidence — rehearsing argument from evidence. This is a responsive teaching exchange whose efficacy here is a proposal; it is best used after learners have constructed an argument so they have something to defend.
sourceClaims: Justifying a classification means citing specific, diagnostic observable characteristics as evidence and distinguishing them from features two similar organisms share (e.g. dolphin vs shark) — an instance of argument from evidence.
learnerActions: State a classification of an organism and your supporting evidence aloud or in writing.
Respond to a taxonomist who probes each justification: 'You say mammal — what's your evidence? The shark also has fins, so why isn't the dolphin a fish?'
Drop any reason the challenger shows is shared or irrelevant, and replace it with a decisive, distinguishing characteristic.
Keep going until you can name a feature present in your claimed group and absent in the look-alike group, and explain why it settles the case.
activities.intendedInsight: A classification must survive challenge: defensible reasons cite characteristics that separate the claimed group from the alternative being compared, and you can discard a reason once you see a similar organism shares it.

activities.title: Worked-example read: shared vs diagnostic features
feedback: If the learner labels a shared feature as the distinguishing one, re-highlight that both animals show it.
Confirm when the learner isolates the feature present in one group and absent in the other.
activities.rationale: A worked example of one contrast can pre-teach the shared-vs-diagnostic distinction. It presents the reasoning rather than having the learner construct it, so it works as a scaffold or pre-read, not as the main task.
sourceClaims: Justifying a classification means citing specific, diagnostic observable characteristics as evidence and distinguishing them from features two similar organisms share (e.g. dolphin vs shark) — an instance of argument from evidence.
learnerActions: Study an annotated comparison of two look-alikes (e.g. dolphin vs shark), where features the two share are marked one way and the features that distinguish them (e.g. lungs vs gills, feeding young on milk) are marked another.
Name, for that pair, which observed features are shared and which features separate the groups.
Explain in your own words why the shared features cannot decide the classification.
activities.intendedInsight: Before constructing an argument, learners can see explicitly that some observed features are shared (non-deciding) while others are diagnostic.

activities.title: Check: which evidence is decisive?
feedback: For a shared-feature distractor, note that the look-alike also has it, so it cannot distinguish the groups — e.g. 'both have four legs' does not separate two four-legged animals.
For an irrelevant feature (colour, size, name), note it varies widely within groups and is not what defines membership of the group.
Confirm selections that name features present in the target group and absent in the alternative.
activities.rationale: Justification is assessable, and items centred on choosing decisive evidence and rejecting shared/irrelevant features check understanding of the standard. Selecting a reason is thinner than constructing and defending one, so this complements rather than replaces the production tasks.
sourceClaims: DfE Y6 'Living things and their habitats' requires pupils to give reasons for classifying plants and animals based on specific characteristics.
learnerActions: For a classified organism, select the TWO characteristics that best justify the classification (multi-select).
Match organism pairs to a feature that distinguishes their groups.
Judge whether a given reason is decisive or merely shared/irrelevant (e.g. is 'lives in the sea' good evidence that something is a fish?).
Critique a wrong justification built on a shared or irrelevant feature and say what makes it weak.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising which evidence is diagnostic reinforces the standard for a good classification argument; recognising a reason is not the same as independently constructing and defending one.

constraints: Require at least two pieces of decisive evidence per classification — a reason, not just a placement — to meet the 'give reasons' standard.
A distinguishing/diagnostic feature must be present in one group and absent in the other; a feature two look-alikes share cannot settle which group each belongs to.
Use convergent look-alikes (dolphin/shark, bat/bird, whale/fish) so learners must reject shared features and find the distinguishing one.

Match cited group diagnostics to the actual organism and life stage used: 'gills' is a larval feature for most amphibians (adults usually breathe through lungs and/or moist skin, and some salamanders have no lungs), though some, such as the neotenic axolotl, keep external gills as adults; gills are shared with fish, so they cannot by themselves decide amphibian vs fish. Confirm each diagnostic against the specific organism rather than applying it as a blanket rule.
The annotated worked-example comparison presents the reasoning; it is a scaffold or pre-read and does not itself have the learner construct and defend an argument, which is the point of the topic.
Selected-response checks verify recognition of decisive evidence but do not elicit an independently constructed, defended justification; pair them with production tasks.
The Socratic dialogue is responsive teaching; use it after learners have produced an argument so they have a claim to defend.
US NGSS does not teach taxonomy at this stage; the content anchor is DfE Y6, while the transferable skill is the NGSS argument-from-evidence practice.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source marks the second claim (diagnostic evidence / dolphin-vs-shark as argument from evidence) as verified:false; treat the specific framing as unconfirmed, though it is consistent with general primary-science guidance.

The original source asserted that 3D 'adds nothing' and that selecting a reason is inherently 'thinner' than constructing one; the first is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, and has been dropped. The recognition/construction distinction is retained only as an objective limit (recognition does not itself elicit independent construction), with the relative efficacy of the dialogue and sim left as a proposal.

Biology examples should be checked against the exact organism and life stage. 'Feeds young on milk / breathes air' distinguishes mammals from fish at this level, but note edge cases: monotreme mammals lay eggs yet still feed young milk; most amphibians have gills only as larvae while the axolotl keeps external gills as an adult. Teachers should confirm each diagnostic fits the specific creature used.

probeDeeper: Do other groups also live in water? So does 'lives in water' really prove it's a fish?
Which single feature, if you covered it up, would leave you unsure of the group?
You gave one reason — what is a second, independent piece of evidence?
These two look almost identical — what is the one feature that puts them in different groups?
assess.correctAnswer: Selects diagnostic, observable characteristics (e.g. fur + gives live young → mammal; moist skin + gills → amphibian) and cites at least two as evidence for the decision. When comparing look-alikes, isolates the feature that truly distinguishes the groups (scales vs fur, gills vs lungs) rather than a shared superficial one (both swim).

errorPatterns.pattern: Justifies by surface resemblance or habitat, not diagnostic features — 'it lives in water, so it's a fish.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'do other groups also do that?'; steer to a feature that only the claimed group has (gills, scales) before accepting the classification.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cites 'swims / lives in water' as the evidence for a group.

errorPatterns.pattern: Asserts a group with only one feature, or none — 'it's just a mammal.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: 'what can you actually SEE that tells you?' and require a second, independent feature. The group knowledge is present; the justification habit needs prompting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States a group but offers fewer than two observable reasons.

errorPatterns.pattern: In the compare task, picks a feature the two animals SHARE ('both have four legs') instead of one that distinguishes them.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt for a feature where the two DIFFER; a distinguishing feature must be present in one group and absent in the other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names a non-diagnostic shared trait when asked what separates the look-alikes.

responseLevels.gap: Classifies on surface impression or habitat and offers no discriminating evidence.
responseLevels.full: Justifies with two or more diagnostic observable features and, comparing look-alikes, names the precise feature that separates the groups — reasoning from evidence rather than first impressions.
responseLevels.partial: Reaches the right group and gives one observable reason, but the second is weak or shared, or cannot isolate the feature that separates look-alikes.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a photo of an unfamiliar animal (e.g. a pangolin or an axolotl) and one or two look-alikes. Set the task and watch: 'Decide which group this animal belongs to, and convince me using only what you can actually see — give me at least two features as your evidence. Then compare it with this similar-looking animal and tell me the one feature that settles which group each is in.' Do not supply features yourself.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the justification reveals whether the child reasons FROM observable, discriminating evidence, or classifies on first impression and then hunts for support. The compare task exposes whether they can find the feature that genuinely separates two similar organisms, versus naming traits the two share.
